title: Vector store options compared
summary: Azure AI Search, Cosmos DB for NoSQL, PostgreSQL, Redis, Qdrant, Pinecone, Elasticsearch and OpenSearch can all hold vectors. The right one depends on where the data lives, filters and hybrid search, scale and who runs it.
useIf: You are picking where vectors live, or checking whether the store you have still fits its scale and filters.
avoidIf: You would choose by a vendor benchmark. Compare on your own vectors, filters and operating model.

explain.md: Most stores offer the same core idea (an ANN index with filters) and differ in the surrounding system. Decide with these dials: **vector count**, **memory budget**, **write and delete rate**, **filter selectivity**, whether you need **keyword (BM25) and hybrid search in the same engine**, **data gravity** (vectors beside transactional data), **tenancy model** and **who operates it**.

explain.title: Where to start
explain.alt: If the data already lives in PostgreSQL use pgvector or pg_diskann. If it lives in Cosmos DB for NoSQL use its vector index. If you need documents, hybrid search, filters and managed ingestion use Azure AI Search. If scale or self-hosting control dominates consider a specialist store.

explain.md: **Data gravity** often decides it. If the source of truth is PostgreSQL, pgvector avoids a second system, a sync pipeline and a consistency gap. If documents flow in from storage and users need keyword plus vector search with filters, a search service with indexers and skillsets removes work you would otherwise build. When vector counts reach hundreds of millions, memory-frugal indexes (DiskANN, quantization) and operating cost take over. Whatever you choose, confirm the hard limits first (dimension caps, minimum vector counts, whether the index policy can be changed) because they decide what is possible before performance does.

pitfalls.symptom: A Cosmos DB vector policy change is rejected
pitfalls.cause: Vector policies cannot be edited in place
pitfalls.fix: Design dimensions and index type upfront, or drop and re-add the policy and re-index

pitfalls.symptom: Behaviour differs from the documentation you read
pitfalls.cause: Defaults change by version, for example Elasticsearch index types for floats
pitfalls.fix: Check the version you run and pin it

pitfalls.symptom: The team cannot keep a second vector system in sync with the database
pitfalls.cause: A separate store was added without a change pipeline or consistency plan
pitfalls.fix: Use the database's own vector support, or build change capture and reconciliation first

scenarios.title: Enterprise documents, small platform team
scenarios.situation: An Azure-based company indexes 20 million chunks from files and wikis. Users need keyword plus vector search with filters and per-group access. The platform team is small.
scenarios.question: Which store do you choose?

options.name: Azure AI Search with indexers, skillsets and pre-filtering
options.why: It gives keyword and vector search, filters, quantization and managed ingestion in one service, which fits a small team.
options.tradeoff: A memory-based quota and some access-control features still in preview.

options.name: PostgreSQL with pgvector
options.why: Familiar SQL and a single database.
options.tradeoff: You build ingestion, keyword ranking and filter tuning yourself.

options.name: Self-hosted Qdrant
options.why: A small team would run and patch another system and build ingestion around it.
options.tradeoff: Right when control, on-premises hosting or a vector-first workload justify the operations.

flips.if: The data already lives in PostgreSQL and joins are essential

flips.then: Evaluate Qdrant, OpenSearch or Elasticsearch with an operations plan.

scenarios.takeaway: A managed search service removes pipeline work from a small team.

scenarios.title: Transactional app already on PostgreSQL
scenarios.situation: A product catalogue of 2 million rows lives in PostgreSQL with row-level security and many joins. The team adds semantic search over descriptions and wants one source of truth.
unknowns: How selective are the common filters?
scenarios.question: Where do the vectors go?

options.name: pgvector in the same database with HNSW and iterative scans
options.why: Vectors sit beside the rows, security and joins apply as usual and there is no sync pipeline.
options.tradeoff: You tune filters and own scaling.

options.name: Sync the rows into AI Search
options.tradeoff: A second system, sync lag and permissions that must be mirrored.

options.name: Move to a dedicated vector database and rebuild joins in application code
options.why: Gives up relational features the app relies on, for scale it does not need.
options.tradeoff: Right if vectors outgrow PostgreSQL by orders of magnitude.

flips.if: Vectors grow to hundreds of millions
Hybrid keyword ranking becomes the main need

scenarios.takeaway: Keep vectors beside the data when scale allows.

scenarios.title: Operational documents in Cosmos DB
scenarios.situation: A multi-tenant application stores JSON documents in Cosmos DB for NoSQL, partitioned by tenant. It adds semantic search and wants vectors with the documents.
constraints: Cosmos DB is the source of truth
Several million documents per partition set
unknowns: Does the embedding model change soon?
scenarios.question: How do you add vector search?

options.name: Add a vector policy with a `diskANN` index on the container, decided upfront
options.why: Vectors stay with the documents, 1,536 dimensions are within the 4,096 limit and tenancy follows the partition key.
options.tradeoff: The policy cannot be edited later and approximate indexes need at least 1,000 vectors.

options.name: Copy documents into AI Search through an indexer
options.why: Rich search features and managed ingestion.
options.tradeoff: A second copy, sync lag and costs for both services.

options.name: Use a `flat` index
options.why: It supports only up to 505 dimensions, so 1,536-dimension vectors do not fit.
options.tradeoff: Right for small sets of low-dimension vectors where exact search is wanted.

flips.if: The embedding model or dimensions may change
flips.then: Plan for dropping and re-adding the vector policy with a rebuild.
Check the 1,000 vector minimum per approximate index.

scenarios.takeaway: Know the store's hard limits before committing to its index type.

quiz.q: Match each store to a documented fact.

pairs.r: Namespaces per index range from 100 to 1,000,000 by plan
FLAT for under 1M vectors, HNSW above

quiz.explain: Each limit comes from the store's documentation. The numbers differ, so a design that fits one store may need change in another.

quiz.q: A team with a Postgres source of truth, 2 million rows and row-level security needs semantic search. What is the usual best first move?
options: Migrate to a dedicated vector database
Add pgvector to the same database
Build a custom index in application memory
Switch to a larger embedding model only
quiz.explain: Data gravity and a small corpus favour keeping vectors beside the rows. A dedicated store adds sync and loses relational features, a custom index is unnecessary work, and a larger model does not address where vectors live.

flashcards.front: What dials decide the vector store?
flashcards.back: Vector count, memory budget, write and delete rate, filter selectivity, hybrid search needs, data gravity, tenancy and who operates it.

flashcards.front: What are Cosmos DB for NoSQL vector index limits?
flashcards.back: `flat` up to 505 dimensions, `quantizedFlat` and `diskANN` up to 4,096, with at least 1,000 vectors for approximate indexes. Policies cannot be edited in place.
`vector` up to 2,000, `halfvec` up to 4,000 and binary quantization up to 64,000. `pg_diskann` indexes up to 16,000 from version 0.6.

flashcards.front: Why can data gravity beat feature lists?
flashcards.back: Vectors beside the source rows avoid a second system, a sync pipeline and permission mirroring.
